task.title: Deploying the into Amazon EKS cluster
task.shortdesc: Deploy the into your cluster and configure it to be able to connect to your queue managers. Deploying the creates a pod with two containers: one for the and one for a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that connects to your queue managers

ul.li: Ensure that you meet the requirements and that you completed the previous steps listed in .

Install the following command-line utilities in your cluster (the instructions in this task use commands, though you can use your container environment’s web interface if you prefer):
oc. For more information, see the documentation for your version of . For example, Getting started with the OpenShift CLI.
helm version 3 or above. For more information, see the same page in the
documentation.
Container Registry CLI. For more information, see Setting up the Container Registry CLI and namespace in the documentation.
Deploy the into your cluster. This software is required for monitoring license usage of queue managers. For instructions, see Deploying License Service

context.p: In this task, you create the objects in your cluster that the requires to connect to your installation and instance of . You can create objects by using either the console or the CLI. The following steps use the CLI.

You start by creating the following objects:
A ConfigMap object that contains information about your queue managers, in the form of a client channel definition table (CCDT)
Secret objects that contain credentials and keys for secure connections
An override file, to override some of the default values for the configuration properties

You then deploy the , which creates more objects in your cluster, including a pod with containers for the following components:
The .
An MCP server that uses an client with your CCDT ConfigMap to connect to your queue managers. An MCP server is a program that connects AI agents to external data, tools, and systems. For more information, see Understanding MCP servers in the Model Context Protocol documentation.
The embedding foundation model that the uses to answer
documentation questions. For more information, see .
For more information about config maps and secrets, see the documentation for your version of . For example, Creating and using config maps and Providing sensitive data to pods by using secrets.

step.cmd: Log in to your cluster by using the oc command. For more information, see the documentation for your version of .
step.info: For example, Logging in to the OpenShift CLI.

step.cmd: Switch to the namespace (project) where you want to deploy the .
In your cluster, create, a Secret object to contain your key for pulling software from the Container Registry.
step.info: They key must be an image pull secret called ibm-entitlement-key. The key will be used during deployment to pull the and images from the Container Registry.

substep.cmd: Get the entitlement key that is assigned to your ID. Log in to My IBM Container Software Library with the ID and password that are associated with the entitled software.
In the Entitlement keys section, click Copy to copy the entitlement key to the clipboard.

step.info: From the CLI, run the following command to create an image pull secret called ibm-entitlement-key.oc create secret docker-registry ibm-entitlement-key \ --docker-server=cp.icr.io \ --docker-username=cp \ --docker-password=<entitlement_key> \ --docker-email=<user_email> \ --namespace=<namespace>where <entitlement_key> is the entitlement key that you copied earlier, <user_email> is the IBMID that is associated with the entitled software, and <namespace> is the namespace where you are deploying the .

step.cmd: Create a ConfigMap object to contain information about the queue managers that you want the to work with.
step.info: This information is used by the MCP server to connect to your queue managers.

substep.cmd: Create an client channel definition table (CCDT), in JSON format.
Edit the file to replace the contents with your own information.
substep.info:
Add an entry for each of the queue managers that you granted access for in .
Do not add more than 20 queue managers in the CCDT; higher numbers impact performance. If you exceed this limit, the MCP server MCP server does not start and an error is generated in the MCP server container log.
Do not use queue manager groups or duplicate queue manager names in the CCDT; such names are ignored by the MCP server.
Do not use asterisks in queue manager names in the CCDT. The MCP server finds such names ambiguous when you use them the MCP server chat assistant, leading to clarification questions.

substep.cmd: Create the ConfigMap from the JSON file
substep.info: For example, run the following command:oc create configmap my-ccdt --from-file=ccdt.json=my-ccdt.json

step.cmd: If queue manager connections in your CCDT require a password to connect, create a Secret object to contain the necessary credentials.
step.info: The MCP server MCP server uses these credentials when it connects to the queue managers. The secret must contain a key called my-mcp-configuration, with a value that lists the username and password for each connection.

substep.stepxmp: Copy the following .ini file template and save it as a local file called my-mcpconfig.ini:[mqenv] # Default username and password for client connectivity to IBM MQ queue managers # (you can override this for individual queue managers, as shown in the following section) username = mq-username password = mq-password # To override connection information for an individual queue manager # Provide one or more stanzas in the form [QM:<name>] [QM:QM1] username=<QM1-username> password=<QM1-password> [routes] # Enable /health custom route for generic health check of running MCP server health = enabled

substep.cmd: Edit the file to replace the username and stanza details with your own information (leave the [routes] and following lines).
Create the Secret object from the .ini file.
substep.stepxmp: For example, run the following command:oc create secret generic my-mcp-configuration --from-file=mcpconfig.ini=my-mcpconfig.ini

step.cmd: If queue manager connections in your CCDT require a TLS connection, create a Secret object to contain a keystore with the necessary keys.
step.info: The MCP server MCP server uses this keystore when it connects to the queue managers.

substep.cmd: Create a PKCS#12 keystore called mcpserver.p12, and record the password that you set for the keystore.
substep.info: The keystore must be a valid PKCS#12 keystore for use with .

substep.cmd: Create the following keys then import them into the keystore:

ul.li: Public keys for the queue managers that you want the to interact with
A public and private key for the MCP server (the client application)

substep.cmd: Create the Secret object from the mcpserver.p12 file:
substep.info: For example, run the following command to create a secret called agent-qm-keystore:oc create secret generic agent-qm-keystore --from-file=keystore.p12=mcpserver.p12

step.cmd: Create a Secret object to contain a TLS key for the to use to connect to the .
step.info:
The
communicates with the agent by using an HTTPS API endpoint, which needs a key and a certificate. You must create a TLS Kubernetes Secret with the keys tls.key, tls.crt, and ca.crt. You also need the ca.crt file for configuring the .

substep.cmd: For testing purposes, you could create a self-signed certificate with OpenSSL.
substep.info: Create a certificate authority:openssl genpkey -algorithm rsa -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:4096 -out "ca.key" openssl req -x509 -new -nodes -key "ca.key" -sha512 -days 30 -subj "/CN=selfsigned-ca" -out "ca.crt" Generate a certificate, replacing <cluster_name> with the name of your cluster.:openssl req -new -nodes -out "cert.csr" -newkey rsa:4096 -keyout "cert.key" -subj "/CN=*.apps.<cluster_name>" openssl x509 -req -in "cert.csr" -CA "ca.crt" -CAkey "ca.key" -CAcreateserial -out "cert.crt" -days 30 -sha512

substep.cmd: Create a TLS Kubernetes Secret object called mq-agent-tls from the key and certificate.
substep.info: Run the following command:oc create secret generic mq-agent-tls --type="kubernetes.io/tls" --from-file=tls.key=cert.key --from-file=tls.crt=cert.crt --from-file=ca.crt

step.cmd: Provide access to the Helm chart in the Helm chart repository.

ul.li: If you already have the Helm chart repository, run the following command to update it: helm repo update ibm-helm
If you do not have the Helm chart repository, run the following command to add it: helm repo add ibm-helm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IBM/charts/master/repo/ibm-helm

step.cmd: Create an overrides file to override some of the default values for the configuration properties.
step.info:
The default values are set in the values.yaml file in the Helm chart package. You must override some of the values, for example license.license and license.accept, which specify the license that you are entitled to and whether you accept it. You can also specify that the
connects to a AI runtime instead of the default, .
To override the default values, create a new YAML file called overrides.yaml, then add to that file the properties that you want to override, along with their new values. You will specify the overrides.yaml file when you install the . You might also need the overrides.yaml when you upgrade the agent.
For a list of values that you can set, including which values are required, see . If you want to see the default values, you can download the values.yaml file by using Helm; for more information, see helm get values in the Helm documentation.
step.stepxmp: An example overrides.yaml file:license: accept: true license: metadata: annotations: productID: "208423bb063c43288328b1d788745b0c" productName: "IBM MQ Advanced" productMetric: "PROCESSOR_VALUE_UNIT" productChargedContainers: "All" agent: model: providers: myWatsonxRuntime: watsonxService: projectID: my-watsonx-project key: my-watsonx-project-key mcpServer: ccdtConfigMapName: my-ccdt keyStoreSecretName: agent-qm-keystore keyStorePassword: <mcpserver.p12_keystore_password> configurationSecretName: my-mcp-configuration route: enabled: true

step.cmd: Deploy the by using the helm install command.
step.stepxmp: helm install <release_name> ibm-helm/ibm-mq-agent --values overrides.yamlwhere <release_name> is a name that you choose for the release, for example ibm-mq-agent.

result.p: The Helm deployment creates the following objects in your cluster:

ul.li:
A pod with three containers: one for the itself, one for the MCP server, and one for the embedding foundation model that the uses for
documentation questions.
A pod with two containers: one for the itself and one for the MCP server
A service for connecting to the from within the cluster
Optional: A Route for connecting to the from outside the cluster
A secret that contains your or credentials
A secret that contains an client INI file, with the keystore password
A secret with a generated API key for the to use to access the
A ServiceAccount for the pod to use. No access to the Kubernetes API is required by the pod
A NetworkPolicy to protect network traffic that flows to the pod

postreq.p:
Check that your installation was successful.
Ensure that you are connected to your project:oc project <your project name>
Watch the pod status to ensure that the new pod starts successfully:oc get pods -wThe STATUS should be Running and the pod name should be followed by 3/32/2, which indicates that all the deployed containers are running. For example:NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE ibm-mq-agent-mq-agent-79565f867c-p2d5j 3/32/2 Running 0 1hPress Ctrl+C to stop watching.
Optionally, you can run the following command to get the pod details, including the two containers that were deployed (agent and mcp-server). oc describe pod <your pod name>
Examine the container logs to check that the running applications started correctly. Note that the containers might take 1 to 2 minutes to start, complete their initial setup tasks, then establish connectivity. During this time, you might observe error messages in the logs because service dependencies are not yet available.
For the agent container: oc logs <your pod name> -c agent | grep -A 2 -B 2 "Application startup complete" You should see output similar to the following:INFO : Initializing API server INFO : Agent Build Info: {'commit_id': '5e9b78a', 'build_version': 'v1.0.0'} INFO: Application startup complete. INFO: Uvicorn running on https://0.0.0.0:8001 (Press CTRL+C to quit) INFO : 10.254.24.2:52616 - New thread ID created: TD_2ad15dd3-18b3-4139-b761-081aaf40dc89
For the mcp-server container:oc logs ibm-mq-agent-ibm-mq-agent-6f6f48d85-qz4kn -c mcp-server | grep -A 2 -B 2 "Application startup complete" You should see output similar to the following:INFO: Started server process [5] INFO: Waiting for application startup. INFO: Application startup complete. INFO: Uvicorn running on http://0.0.0.0:8000 (Press CTRL+C to quit) INFO: 10.254.20.2:42122 - "GET /health HTTP/1.1" 200 OK Need similar for the Embedding container

If the logs contain errors, fix the problem then retry. For example, the following error message in the MCP server log indicates that you have too many queue managers in your CCDT:CCDT contains 22 queue managers, which exceeds the recommended maximum of 20.Correct the CCDT, refresh the ConfigMap object, then restart the pod.
For more information about error logs, see
When the pod is running as expected, proceed to .
